summary.text: Letting \(D\) denote decimal digit sum, set \(d=D(n)\), \(e=D(d)\), and \(q=(n-e)/9\); digit-sum congruence modulo \(9\) makes \(q\) integral, and when \(q>0\) a digit-sum bound gives \(d\le 10^q\). The padded digits of \(d-1\) and their \(9\)-complements form a block of digit sum \(9q\) divisible by \(d\); adjoining zeros and the digits of \(d\) produces a distinct \(k\) with \(d\mid k\) and \(D(k)=9q+e=n\), while the case \(q=0\) is handled by \(k=10n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(x)\) denote the sum of the ordinary base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
It will then follow immediately that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty, so its least member is positive and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We use a few elementary facts about decimal digits. First,
\[
D(x)\le x
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(x\). For positive \(x\), we also have \(D(x)>0\), since its decimal expansion has at least one nonzero digit. Appending a zero on the right does not change digit sum, so
\[
D(10x)=D(x).
\]
Finally, every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its digit sum:
\[
x\equiv D(x)\pmod 9.
\]
Applying this last fact twice gives
\[
x\equiv D(D(x))\pmod 9. \tag{1}
\]

We first establish a decimal-block construction that will be used in the main proof. Decimal digit lists below are written from least significant digit to most significant digit. If \(B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1})\), write
\[
\operatorname{val}(B)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}b_i10^i.
\]
For concatenated lists one consequently has
\[
\operatorname{val}(B\mathbin{\|}C)
 =\operatorname{val}(B)+10^{|B|}\operatorname{val}(C). \tag{2}
\]

**Decimal-block lemma.** Suppose \(d>0\) and \(d\le 10^m\). Then there is a list \(L\) of decimal digits such that
\[
\sum_{x\in L}x=9m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 d\mid\operatorname{val}(L). \tag{3}
\]

To prove this, write \(d-1\) as a block \(A\) of exactly \(m\) decimal digits, allowing leading zeros. This is possible because
\[
0\le d-1<10^m.
\]
Thus \(|A|=m\) and \(\operatorname{val}(A)=d-1\). Let \(C\) be the digitwise 9-complement of \(A\): each digit \(x\) of \(A\) is replaced by \(9-x\). Then
\[
\sum C=9m-\sum A. \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, if \(A=(a_0,\ldots,a_{m-1})\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{val}(C)
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(9-a_i)10^i\\
 &=9\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}10^i-\operatorname{val}(A)\\
 &=(10^m-1)-(d-1)=10^m-d. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Take \(L=C\mathbin{\|}A\). Every entry of \(L\) is a decimal digit. By (4),
\[
\sum L=\sum C+\sum A=9m.
\]
Using (2), (5), and \(|C|=m\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{val}(L)
 &=\operatorname{val}(C)+10^m\operatorname{val}(A)\\
 &=(10^m-d)+10^m(d-1)\\
 &=d(10^m-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(d\mid\operatorname{val}(L)\), proving the lemma.

We next derive the estimate that will ensure the hypothesis \(d\le10^m\) in the relevant application. For every positive \(x\),
\[
D(x)\le \frac{x-D(x)}9+9, \tag{6}
\]
where the quotient denotes integer division. To see this, write
\[
x=10t+r,\qquad 0\le r\le9.
\]
Then
\[
D(x)=D(t)+r\le t+r.
\]
It follows that
\[
x-D(x)=10t+r-(D(t)+r)=10t-D(t)\ge9t,
\]
because \(D(t)\le t\). Therefore
\[
t\le\left\lfloor\frac{x-D(x)}9\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(D(x)=D(t)+r\le t+9\), inequality (6) follows.

We will also use the elementary inequality
\[
q+9\le10^q\qquad(q\ge1). \tag{7}
\]
For \(q=1\), both sides are \(10\). If it holds for some \(q\ge1\), then
\[
(q+1)+9=q+10\le10(q+9)\le10^{q+1};
\]
the first inequality is immediate for \(q\ge1\). Thus (7) follows by induction.

Now fix a positive integer \(n\), and put
\[
d=D(n),\qquad e=D(d),\qquad q=\frac{n-e}{9}.
\]
Because \(n>0\), we have \(d>0\), and hence \(e>0\). Also
\[
e=D(d)\le d=D(n)\le n. \tag{8}
\]
By (1), \(n\equiv e\pmod9\). In view of \(e\le n\), this says that \(9\mid n-e\). Consequently the displayed quotient defining \(q\) is exact, and
\[
n=e+9q. \tag{9}
\]
We split into two cases.

### Case 1: \(q=0\)

Equation (9) gives \(n=e\). Combining this with (8),
\[
n=e\le d\le n,
\]
so \(d=n\) as well. Take
\[
k=10n.
\]
This is positive and, since \(n>0\), it is strictly larger than \(n\), so \(k\ne n\). Furthermore,
\[
D(n)=d=n\mid10n=k.
\]
Appending a zero does not alter digit sum, and hence
\[
D(k)=D(10n)=D(n)=n,
\]
which certainly divides \(n\). Thus \(k\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

### Case 2: \(q>0\)

We first show that
\[
d\le10^q. \tag{10}
\]
Since \(e=D(d)\le d=D(n)\), subtraction from \(n\) gives
\[
n-D(n)\le n-e.
\]
After integer division by \(9\),
\[
\frac{n-D(n)}9\le\frac{n-e}{9}=q.
\]
Applying (6) to \(n\), we obtain
\[
d=D(n)\le\frac{n-D(n)}9+9\le q+9.
\]
As \(q>0\), inequality (7) now yields (10).

Apply the decimal-block lemma with \(m=q\) and this positive integer \(d\). We obtain a list \(L\) of decimal digits such that
\[
\sum L=9q,
\qquad d\mid\operatorname{val}(L). \tag{11}
\]
Let \(G\) be a block of \(n+1\) zero digits, and let \(H\) be the ordinary decimal digit list of \(d\), again in least-significant-first order. Form the concatenated digit list
\[
K=L\mathbin{\|}G\mathbin{\|}H

y\]
and let
\[
k=\operatorname{val}(K).
\]
(The stray symbol in the preceding display is immaterial; explicitly, the intended definition is \(K=L\mathbin{\|}G\mathbin{\|}H\).)

Every entry of \(K\) is between \(0\) and \(9\). Its digit sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum K
 &=\sum L+\sum G+\sum H\\
 &=9q+0+D(d)\\
 &=9q+e=n,
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]
where the last equality is (9). Since \(d>0\), its usual decimal list \(H\) is nonempty and has a nonzero most significant digit. Thus the concatenated list \(K\) is a valid decimal expansion of \(k\) (the zero block merely separates its lower and upper portions). Therefore (12) gives
\[
D(k)=n. \tag{13}
\]
In particular, \(k>0\), since its digit sum is the positive number \(n\). Equation (13) also immediately gives
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{14}
\]

It remains to prove both that \(d\mid k\) and that \(k\ne n\). For divisibility, repeated use of the concatenation identity (2) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
k
 &=\operatorname{val}(L\mathbin{\|}G)
   +10^{|L|+|G|}\operatorname{val}(H)\\
 &=\operatorname{val}(L)
   +10^{|L|+|G|}d.
\end{aligned} \tag{15}
\]
Here the zero block contributes no value, and \(\operatorname{val}(H)=d\). The first term in (15) is divisible by \(d\) by (11), and the second visibly is as well. Hence
\[
d=D(n)\mid k. \tag{16}
\]

Finally, suppose for contradiction that \(k=n\). From (13) we would then have
\[
D(n)=D(k)=n,
\]
so \(d=n\). It would follow that
\[
e=D(d)=D(n)=n.
\]
But (9) would then read
\[
n=n+9q,
\]
which is impossible because \(q>0\). Therefore \(k\ne n\). Together, (13), (14), and (16) show that this \(k\) is a positive Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

We have now produced such a partner in both cases. Hence, for every positive \(n\), the set
\[
P_n=\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and that least element is still positive. By definition, \(a(n)\) is this least element whenever \(P_n\) is nonempty, and is \(0\) only when \(P_n\) is empty. Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)\ne0.
\]
